items.title: Joseph Fletcher's situation ethics centres on agape
items.claim: What is the central principle of Fletcher's situation ethics?

options.text: There are no moral rules whatsoever
The single absolute is agape (selfless love); all other rules are guidelines that can be overridden when love requires. Set out in 'Situation Ethics: The New Morality' (1966)
Maximise pleasure for the greatest number

items.reveal:
Fletcher's six propositions: (1) Only love is intrinsically good. (2) The ruling norm of Christian decision is love, not law. (3) Love and justice are the same — justice is love distributed. (4) Love wills the neighbour's good. (5) Only the end justifies the means. (6) Love's decisions are made situationally, not prescriptively.

Fletcher's four working principles: pragmatism, relativism, positivism, personalism.

The Vatican condemned situation ethics under Pius XII (1956, before Fletcher's book) and again in the 1990s. Critics argue 'love' as sole criterion is too vague; defenders argue agape has specific New Testament content that excludes self-interested 'love'.
items.why: Christian ethics in the mid-20th century split between absolutist and contextual approaches. Fletcher's situation ethics is a high-profile example of context-driven ethics — challenging the natural law tradition from within Christianity.

items.title: William James identified four marks of mystical experience
items.claim: What are James's four marks of mystical experience?

options.text: Ineffability (cannot be fully described), noetic quality (provides knowledge), transiency (does not last long), passivity (the subject feels acted upon) — set out in 'The Varieties of Religious Experience' (1902)

items.reveal:
James's Gifford Lectures (1901-02) became 'The Varieties of Religious Experience'. He aimed to study religion empirically as a phenomenon of consciousness, regardless of any metaphysical truth claims.

His four marks were intended as descriptive criteria, not arguments for divine reality. Richard Swinburne ('The Existence of God', 1979) and others later used religious experience evidentially — the principle of credulity (we should believe perceptions unless we have reason not to) and the principle of testimony.

Critics including Walter Kaufmann and Steven Katz have argued that mystical experience is heavily shaped by prior cultural framework — a Buddhist's experience is structured by Buddhist concepts.
items.why: Religious experience is studied both descriptively (what do people report?) and evaluatively (what does it prove?). James's framework remains the starting point for both — a century of subsequent debate has built on his typology.

items.title: Samsara, karma and moksha form a connected Hindu framework

options.text: Samsara is the cycle of birth, death and rebirth; karma is the moral causation that drives it; moksha is liberation from the cycle — typically via realisation of the unity of atman and Brahman, or through bhakti devotion
Karma punishes only in this life
Moksha is automatic at death for all souls

items.reveal:
Karma (action) produces fruits (phala) that bind the soul to future rebirths. Bad karma leads to lower rebirths (animal, hell realms); good karma to better ones (human, deva). All rebirth is conditioned and impermanent.

Moksha is the exit from samsara — variously achieved through jnana (knowledge), bhakti (devotion), karma (right action), or yoga (meditation). The Bhagavad Gita presents all four as legitimate paths.

Buddhism shares samsara, karma and liberation concepts but rejects atman — so 'rebirth' in Buddhism is the continuation of a causal stream, not a soul transmigrating.
items.why: Indian-origin religions share a family of concepts that differ in detail but contrast structurally with Abrahamic religions. The cyclic worldview shapes everything from ethics to attitudes toward death.
